source_read: PDF (version of record), International Journal of Drug Policy 21 (2010) 202-207, all 6 pages; text extracted with pdftotext -layout; pages 202-206 rendered at 150 dpi to check every number, and Fig. 1 (the two vignettes, an image) read at 300 dpi.

claims.overstatement: None for the part from this source; it is worded carefully. Three small precision points. (1) The 'perpetrator-punishment' subscale also contains the two items about expecting him to be violent to himself or others, besides blame, punishment and spiritual or religious referral; 'statements about blame, punishment and non-medical responses' leaves these out. (2) The 'victim-treatment' subscale (alpha .64) also holds biological-cause items (genetic, chemical imbalance) and a severity item, so 'treatment-related statements' is a simplification. (3) 'People at talks on substance use' is accurate, but the paper's own description is mental health care providers (abstract: clinicians), which matters for interpretation; '64.5% with a doctoral-level degree' partly conveys this. Only 34.8% had a professional focus on alcohol or drug problems.
claims.note: This source covers only the Kelly & Westerhoff part of the claim (from 'Words for the person were tested ...' to '... social contact or treatment statements', and the Kelly part of the magnitude). Every number was checked on the rendered pages (pp. 202-205). 728; October 2008; 516; mean age 51; 64.5%; 2.92 (SD 0.57) vs 2.82 (SD 0.58); t = 2.05, 504 df, p = .02; d = 0.20; ps > .59; .025 per comparison: all as printed. Recomputed: one-sided p for t = 2.05 on 504 df = .020, two-sided = .041, so the printed .02 matches an unstated one-sided test, and a two-sided test would need t > 2.25 to pass the authors' .025 level; the hypothesis was directional (p. 203), but no one-sided test is declared. d from the printed means and pooled SD = 0.17 (0.16 to 0.19 allowing for rounding of the means), and 0.18 from t with equal groups, so the printed 0.20 is slightly above what the printed figures allow; 95% CI about 0.01 to 0.36 (0.00 to 0.35 with d = 0.17), matching the editors' calculation. ps > .59 means |t| < 0.54, |d| < 0.05, with intervals reaching about plus or minus 0.22, so differences of the size seen on perpetrator-punishment cannot be ruled out for social threat or victim-treatment, as the claim says. Non-completion 212 of 728 = 29.1%. Also: 504 df implies 506 people in the t-test, not 516 (10 unexplained), and group sizes are not reported. The subscales were derived by exploratory factor analysis of the same responses, not specified in advance; the vignette (Fig. 1, p. 203) describes Mr. Williams attending a treatment programme 'through the court', required to stay abstinent, with two positive urine toxicology screens and a breathalyzer reading a month ago and a further positive urine screen since, awaiting the judge; the two versions differ only in the term used (twice). The conference location is not stated (only the authors' Boston affiliation).

anchors.extracted: Describes a randomized between-subjects cross-sectional vignette design; clinicians (N = 516) at two mental-health conferences (63% female, 81% white, mean age 51, 65% doctoral-level), 71% response. Three subscales: perpetrator-punishment (alpha .80), social threat (.86), victim-treatment (.64). No difference on social threat or victim-treatment; 'substance abuser' readers agreed more with personal culpability and punitive measures. Conclusions call the judgments 'systematically different' and say the term may perpetuate stigmatizing attitudes.

anchors.locator: Method, Study population and protocol, 1st paragraph; Fig. 1
anchors.extracted: 728 mental health care providers attending two mental-health/addiction-focused conferences in October 2008 (location not given); attendees present at the start of two addiction-focused talks were handed one of two survey forms that differed only in the term ('substance abuser' or 'substance use disorder') in a vignette about Mr. Williams, who attends a court treatment programme requiring abstinence and had two positive urine drug screens and a positive breathalyzer reading a month earlier and a further positive urine screen since, and awaits the judge.

anchors.locator: Method, Study population and protocol, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: The two forms were handed out alternately and in sequence by study staff (the authors call this even and random distribution through the auditoria); completion took about 20 minutes; completion rate 71% (516 of 728, so 212 or 29% did not complete); no eligibility or exclusion criteria: all attendees who chose to return the survey.

Items rated 1 (strongly disagree) to 6 (strongly agree), mostly from the 1996 General Social Survey, 8 written by the authors. Promax loadings: factor 1 (14 items) covers blame and choice, disciplinary action, jail, community service, increasing consequences, referral to a religious leader or spiritual healer, God's will, upbringing, and expecting violence to himself or others; factor 2 (4 items): willing to have him as employee, close friend, neighbour, co-worker; factor 3 (8 items): more intensive treatment, family and friends, medication, therapist, self-help group, genetic cause, chemical imbalance, severity.
Checks across the two groups on demographic variables (chi-square and t-tests) found no differences (ps > .17).
Independent t-tests compared the two terms on each of the three subscales; significance level set at .025 per comparison to limit type I error. No one-sided test is mentioned.

516 completers: mean age 51, 63.4% female, 81.0% White, 64.5% doctoral-level degree; professional focus on mood (66.9%), anxiety (59.9%), psychosis (37%), alcohol or drug problems (34.8%). Three factors explained 33% of variance; subscales of 14 items (alpha .80), 4 items (.86) and 8 items (.64), labelled perpetrator-punishment, social threat and victim-treatment; one item loading on two factors was dropped.

No significant difference between terms on social threat or victim-treatment (ps > .59). Perpetrator-punishment: 'substance use disorder' M 2.82 (SD 0.58) vs 'substance abuser' M 2.92 (SD 0.57), t = 2.05, 504 df, p printed .02, d printed 0.20 (small). Editors' recomputation: one-sided p .020, two-sided .041; d 0.17-0.18, 95% CI about 0.01 to 0.36; 504 df implies 506 analysed; group sizes not reported.

Authors note the difference was small; whether differences on these scales translate into real-world decisions is unknown; the 71% response rate was less than ideal and reasons for non-completion are unknown, so generalisation needs caution; the subscales need confirming in other samples; respondents may have given clinically desirable answers.

risk_of_bias.note: High overall is right: allocation by alternation, known to the staff, with the form in hand before people decided to take part, and 29% non-completion by unknown version. Recorded as design 'rct' with RoB 2, which judges a non-random sequence as high risk. Strictly, alternation makes this a quasi-randomized experiment, which Cochrane guidance also allows to be assessed as a non-randomized study (ROBINS-I). Either way the risk is high, and this evidence should not count as randomized when the claim's certainty is rated. 'Selection of the reported result' could reasonably be high rather than some concerns: the outcome scales were derived after data collection and the one-sided test is unstated. The overall judgment does not change.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial is right. The abstract's 'systematically different judgments' and the call for institutions to change terms rest on one of three post hoc subscales, with d about 0.17-0.18, two-sided p about .041 and alternating allocation; help-seeking, which the Conclusions invoke, was not measured.

missed: Minor: the Results present the four highest figures for 'perpetrator-punishment' (.69, .59, .53, .51, p. 205) as items 'most highly correlated' with the subscale, but they are the Promax pattern loadings of Table 1 rounded (.691, .586, .525, .506, p. 204), not item-subscale correlations. KF 7 repeats the figures correctly but calls them associations.
